title: Setup and hands
hook: 3.5 mm (E-4) for toys; 5.0 mm (H-8) for learning swatches
yarn: #4 worsted cotton for toys; smooth light-colored #4 acrylic for swatches
summary: Get the right kit, set up a chair and a habit that your hands can keep for years, and finish one toy from a beginner kit.
intro: This short course gets you ready for a long, enjoyable hobby. You buy a small toy-focused kit, learn to sit and hold the hook so your hands stay comfortable, and finish a first toy with a guided kit. If you've already finished a beginner kit toy, you can test out of unit 1.0 by checking it against the pass list.
outcomes: You can read a yarn label and choose a smooth, light-colored #4 yarn and a hook sized in millimeters for a toy.
You can set up a practice spot with support, light and a basket, and run a session with warm-up rows and pauses.
You can name the hand warning signs that mean stop for the day and the ones that mean see a clinician.
You have a dated 1-minute side-view video of your hands to compare with later.
You have one finished, stuffed and closed toy.
assessment: Each unit's pass list, checked once in practice and once cold at the start of a later session. Unit 1.0 can be passed by test-out with a toy you already made. The T100.1 hands video is kept and compared again in TOY 190.
reading: The Essential Guide to Amigurumi, by June Gilbank (right- and left-handed editions; price not confirmed): the tools and materials section and the start of Amigurumi 101. Optional in this course; it becomes the core text in TOY 101.

units.time: about 1 hour, plus a shopping trip
units.why: The right yarn and hook make your first stitches easy to see and your first toys dense enough that stuffing stays hidden. A short list keeps the cost down.
units.need: The shopping list below. Craft stores, big-box stores with a craft aisle, and online yarn shops carry all of it.
units.learn: Read your first yarn label with the Craft Yarn Council's How to Read a Yarn Label page (Craft Yarn Council). Then read Nicole Chase's Choosing Amigurumi Crochet Hook Size (Nicole Chase), which explains why toys use a smaller hook than the label suggests. Keep the Craft Yarn Council standards and abbreviations page bookmarked; later units use it. Left-handed: reading labels and buying hooks are the same for both hands. The core textbook, June Gilbank's The Essential Guide to Amigurumi (PlanetJune; price not confirmed), comes in a separate left-handed edition, so buy the one for your hand if you buy it.
key: Shopping list for TOY 100 and TOY 101: one 3.5 mm (E-4) hook, ideally with a soft ergonomic handle; one 5.0 mm (H-8) hook for learning swatches; one skein of smooth, light-colored #4 (worsted) acrylic for swatches; two or three skeins of smooth #4 cotton in light, solid colors for toys (mercerized cotton such as Lion Brand 24/7 Cotton splits least); 10 or more locking stitch markers; one bag of polyester fiberfill; a blunt yarn needle (a bent tip helps); small sharp scissors; a ruler or tape measure marked in mm; a notebook or binder; your phone camera.
Optional now: one beginner kit for unit 1.0 (see that unit). Wait on safety eyes until a pattern or kit calls for them.
The weight number on the label is a skein symbol with a number from 0 to 7. Toys in this course use #4 (worsted or aran).
Pick light, solid, smooth yarn. Dark, fuzzy, variegated, chenille and plush yarns hide your stitches, so they wait until TOY 230.
Buy hooks by millimeters. US letters and numbers differ between brands.
The dye lot is printed on the label. Buy all the skeins for one toy in the same color from the same lot, because lots can differ slightly.
Pull yarn from the center of a skein or cake. If it comes as a hank (a long twisted loop), wind it into a ball first.
This course uses US terms. A UK pattern's dc is your sc, UK htr is US hdc, UK tr is US dc, UK ss is US sl st, and UK miss is US skip.

Shop safely. The real Woobles sites are thewoobles.com and help.thewoobles.com. Look-alike domains ending in .it.com and 'free' patterns of studio-owned characters on unknown sites are scams or copies. A real free pattern has a named designer and a home on the designer's own site, Ravelry or Ribblr.
drill: Photograph the label of your toy yarn. Beside the photo, write its weight number, fiber, length per skein (yards and meters), dye lot, and the hook size the label suggests.
Write each hook's size in millimeters on a slip of masking tape around its handle if it isn't printed there.
Put everything in one basket and photograph the basket for your binder.
Make a free account on Ravelry (ravelry.com). You'll use it from TOY 120 on to see other makers' photos of a pattern before you start it.
On a page in your binder, write the US term for each of these UK terms: dc, htr, tr, ss, miss.
pass: Your label notes match the label on all 5 facts (weight number, fiber, length, dye lot, suggested hook)
Every hook in the basket shows its size in mm
The basket photo shows all items on the shopping list, each one visible
Your UK-to-US answers are sc, hdc, dc, sl st and skip (5 of 5)
wrong: The label gives no hook size
Some labels give only a knitting needle size. Use the yarn's weight number instead; for #4 toy yarn, start at 3.5 mm.
Only fuzzy or dark yarn in the store
Order online, or buy one ball of light acrylic for swatches now and the cotton later. The swatches in TOY 101 come first anyway.
A 'free pattern' site asks you to install something or log in with another account
Close it. Use the designers linked in this course, their own sites, Ravelry or Ribblr.
units.new_skill: Yarn and hook literacy for toys

units.why: Toys use small hooks and firm fabric, which ask more of your hands than most crochet. A good chair, a relaxed grip and regular pauses let you enjoy this for years, and a habit spot makes picking it up easy.
units.need: Your basket from unit 0, a chair with a back, a strong lamp, a plain light cloth for your lap (dark if your yarn is light), and your phone.
units.learn: Read Shiny Happy World's The Right Way to Hold a Crochet Hook: Pencil or Knife? (Shiny Happy World). Then watch the first lessons of Tamara Kelly's free Learn to Crochet course at Moogly (right-handed or left-handed) to see the yarn hand at work. Sigoni Macaroni's free Learn to Crochet Masterclass (Sigoni Macaroni) is a second video voice; its left-handed photo steps are only in the paid ebook ($25, as of Oct 2026). For hand health background, see the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons' carpal tunnel syndrome animation (AAOS OrthoInfo). Left-handed: Moogly's left-handed course films every step left-handed; Shiny Happy World's grip post has no left-handed version, so mirror its photos.
key: Sit in a chair with back support, feet flat on the floor or a footrest, and elbows resting on armrests or a cushion.
Raise the work toward your eyes with a cushion on your lap instead of bending your neck down to it.
Use a strong task light. Over 40, or working with dark yarn, add a magnifier or reading glasses.
Grip: try the pencil grip and the knife grip. Keep the one that leaves your wrist straight, with no bend up, down or sideways. Neither grip is more correct.
Hold the hook lightly. Firm toy fabric comes from a smaller hook, never from squeezing. You'll test this in T101.2.

Session template: warm up with 2 or 3 rows or rounds of something you know, and don't judge tension on these. Then focus on the drill for 15 to 25 minutes. Pause for 1 to 2 minutes: open and close your hands, roll your shoulders, look across the room. Then a second focus block, or switch to your toy. End with two lines in your log: what you did and one thing you noticed.
Keep drill time to about 45 to 60 minutes per sitting. Relaxed toy time can run longer as long as the pauses happen. Two 15-minute sessions in a busy week keep the thread going.
An if-then plan makes starting easy. Write one sentence: 'When [a cue, like after dinner on weekdays], I crochet at [a place].' Keep the basket with the current drill and toy at that spot.
It usually takes two to three months before picking up the hook feels automatic. A day off changes nothing.
Ache or tiredness: stop for the day, check your grip and support, use a softer yarn than cotton for a few sessions, and go down a hook size if you were squeezing for density.

Red flags, which mean stop crocheting and see a clinician (primary care first, then a hand surgeon or a certified hand therapist): numbness or tingling that stays or wakes you at night; weakness or dropping things; a finger that catches or locks; pain on the thumb side of the wrist; pain at rest; swelling or warmth; or any pain that lasts more than 1 to 2 weeks. Stretches feel good but they aren't a treatment.
There are no controlled studies of crochet hook designs. This advice follows general hand-tool ergonomics.
drill: Set up your spot: chair, cushion, light, lap cloth, basket. Photograph it.
Write your if-then plan on the first page of your binder.
Using the 5.0 mm hook and acrylic, make a slip knot and a loose chain of about 20 the way Moogly shows it. This is only for the video; unit 1.1 teaches it properly.

Prop your phone at elbow height to your hook-hand side and record 1 minute of yourself chaining, so the video shows your hands, wrists and forearms from the side. Label it with today's date. Keep it; TOY 190 compares it with a new one.
Pause the video at three moments. At each one, check whether your forearm and the back of your hand make a straight line. If not, change grip or raise the work and record 1 more minute.
On another day, run one full session with the template, including both pauses, and write the two log lines.
pass: The dated 1-minute side-view video is saved where you can find it again
In at least 2 of 3 paused frames, the back of your hand lines up with your forearm (no visible bend at the wrist)
Your if-then plan is written in the binder, and the setup photo shows the chair, light and basket
Your log shows one session with a warm-up, two focus blocks or one block and toy time, and a pause between them
You can find the red-flag list in your binder (copy it onto the inside cover)
wrong: Neck or shoulders ache after 20 minutes
Raise the work with a firmer cushion and rest your elbows. Then check the lamp: leaning in to see is a common cause.
Wrist bends in the video
Try the other grip, or hold the hook a little farther from its tip. Record again next session; one change at a time.
Fingers tired from gripping
Loosen your hold until the hook could almost slide out. If the fabric gets loose, that's a hook-size question for T101.2.
Sessions keep getting skipped
Make the plan smaller: one 10-minute session after a cue you already have. Keep the basket set out at the spot.
units.new_skill: Comfortable setup, grip and session rhythm

units.t: Your first weekend: a finished toy from a kit
units.time: 3 to 8 hours over a weekend or several evenings
units.why: A guided kit gives you a finished toy before you study each stitch, so you know where all the drills in TOY 101 lead. Already finished a beginner kit toy? Test out by checking that toy against the pass list below.
units.need: One beginner-level kit. The Woobles Beginner kits come pre-started, with a close-up video for every step (most beginner kits about $25 to $40, as of Oct 2026). No budget for a kit: use the free course in the learn line instead, with your 3.5 mm hook, cotton, markers and fiberfill.
units.learn: Follow your kit's own videos. The Woobles kits (level system, The Woobles) have right- and left-handed versions of every video; start at their quick-start page, and use the Woobles help center if something in the kit is missing or confusing. Free alternative: Nicole Chase's Learn Amigurumi for Beginners 10-day email course (Nicole Chase), whose first project is a small crayon. Nicole Chase's videos are right-handed; no left-handed version, so mirror the right-handed steps or pair them with The Woobles' free left-handed technique pages.
key: Follow the kit exactly this time. You'll learn the why of each step in TOY 101.
Keep the marker the kit gives you in the first stitch of each round, and move it up every round.
Stuff a little at a time, in small teased pieces, until the toy feels firm and springs back when you squeeze it.
Hide yarn ends by pushing the needle into the toy and out the far side, then trimming close so the end pulls back inside.
Keep this toy. You'll compare it with your from-scratch Wooble in T101.3.
drill: Finish the kit toy following its videos.

Finishing ritual (about 2 minutes): photograph the toy in daylight on a plain background. In the binder, record the yarn, hook, date and kit name, plus one line on what you like most and one thing you'd change.
Test-out route: if you already have a finished kit toy, do step 2 with that toy and check it against the pass list.
pass: The toy is finished, stuffed and closed
Squeezed gently in daylight at arm's length, about 12 in (30 cm), no white stuffing shows between stitches
No yarn tails show on the outside
The daylight photo and binder notes are filed
wrong: Stuffing shows when you squeeze
Kits use a set hook, so add a little less stuffing next time. You'll fix density properly in T101.2.
Lost count in a round
Count the stitches since the marker and compare with the number the video shows at the end of that round. Pull back to the marker if it doesn't match.
Lumpy shape
Massage the lumps outward from outside, or pull out a little stuffing with your hook and add it back in smaller pieces.
units.new_skill: Making a whole toy with video guidance
